# Video Lab 6B The Encoding Problem: transcript

Source: `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\09_PRO_DEV\Old bull performance\Video_Transcripts\Video Lab 6B The Encoding Problem.mp4`. Course post: https://www.oldbullperformance.com/products/running-the-room-building-a-performance-operating-system/categories/2160474413/posts/2199109528. Duration: 00:16:23. Machine-generated with faster-whisper small.en, CPU int8. This is an unverified draft; names and technical terms may be misrecognized. Timestamps refer to the downloaded media.

**00:00:00–00:00:23** Okay, welcome to Module 6B Part A. This is the encoding problem. So in this session, we're

**00:00:23–00:00:29** looking at one of the major challenges in leadership, which is interdisciplinary performance

**00:00:29–00:00:36** environment, and understanding that different disciplines often encode the same information

**00:00:36–00:00:42** in very different ways. And this is a critical idea. Quite often, it's not that people disagree

**00:00:42–00:00:48** on the facts. The issue is that they understand those facts through different lenses. Physiotherapists,

**00:00:48–00:00:53** for example, will view the athlete through the lens of tissue tolerance, biological adaptation,

**00:00:53–00:00:58** rehab, progress, etc. Medical practitioners are more likely to assess the athletes when

**00:00:58–00:01:04** overall health perspective. In some cases, they may even have limited practical understanding

**00:01:04–00:01:09** of what we're actually doing beyond their domain. The SNC coach clearly, they're going

**00:01:09–00:01:13** to look at outputs. How do we get the athlete prepared for competition? They're going to

**00:01:13–00:01:18** get them back. Sport scientists, they're going to be looking at loads, exposure. How do we

**00:01:18–00:01:22** get the numbers back to where they need to be? So different lenses, same information but

**00:01:22–00:01:28** a different lens. So the challenge is absolutely clear. We may be looking at the same athlete,

**00:01:28–00:01:33** the same data, but we're not all looking at it in the same way. And if we want to achieve

**00:01:33–00:01:39** long-term sustainability, then that has to change. The only way to achieve sustainable

**00:01:39–00:01:46** interdisciplinary performance is to realign the encoding framework through which information

**00:01:46–00:01:53** is understood. And without question, that is the core job of someone in a leadership

**00:01:53–00:01:59** position. If you're running a department, it's up to you, particularly in a domain where

**00:01:59–00:02:06** you've maybe inherited a dysfunctional system. You've got to get everybody on the same page,

**00:02:06–00:02:13** and this will take time. It takes effort. It'll take discipline. It'll also require a very

**00:02:13–00:02:19** clear process. As in, when we get A, this is what we're going to do. When we get B,

**00:02:19–00:02:25** this is what we're going to do. Now, it sounds kind of simple, but many environments avoid this type

**00:02:25–00:02:32** of conversation simply because it forces people to get off the fence. It forces people to make

**00:02:32–00:02:38** a decision about how they think about something, particularly an injury or how they're going to

**00:02:38–00:02:44** move someone forward. But committing to paper is absolutely critical. Now, we've talked before about

**00:02:45–00:02:50** the freedom associated with discipline. That discipline affords you the ability to say,

**00:02:50–00:02:54** okay, we've got this structure, but for these reasons, we need to move off. We need to do

**00:02:54–00:03:00** something a little bit different. That's fine, but you're making a conifiable decision. It's

**00:03:00–00:03:05** not just going along randomly. Now, let's take a very straight for example. If you've got a 2A

**00:03:05–00:03:10** bicep femme hamstring, you need to know how are we going to assess it? How are we going to

**00:03:10–00:03:14** process it? What are your checkpoints? What's the tempo? What are we expecting day to day?

**00:03:14–00:03:21** What do we expect on day three, on day four, on day five? How many days realistically do you

**00:03:21–00:03:25** expect before you get that athlete back to performance? This is really disciplined work,

**00:03:25–00:03:31** but this is going to help you with the coach. Now, it may not be just a rehab process. It may

**00:03:31–00:03:35** have to do the same idea with performance. How long is it going to take to get someone from

**00:03:35–00:03:41** point A to point B? But having that model to say, hey, coach, we've got a plan. This is it.

**00:03:41–00:03:45** This is the tempo. This is how it's going to work. Giving them checkpoints along the way.

**00:03:46–00:03:51** Absolutely critical because we didn't mention this before. The coach is going to process

**00:03:51–00:03:54** information through a different lens too. They're processing it through the lens and

**00:03:54–00:04:01** availability. I need my people on the field to play. Simple as that. They really don't talk to

**00:04:01–00:04:05** a lot of the rest of it. From a technical perspective, for most coaches, it's really

**00:04:05–00:04:10** like executive summary stuff. Give me the high level where we are. But what I can tell you

**00:04:10–00:04:17** through absolute experience is getting in front by understanding those timeframes and having that

**00:04:17–00:04:22** set up in advance. Again, your group's been able to encode that information in the same way.

**00:04:22–00:04:28** It's going to help you without question. That disciplined system really means that,

**00:04:28–00:04:34** and what I'm aiming for, is that all of your staff, your S&C, your medical staff, your PT staff,

**00:04:34–00:04:40** physiotherapy, et cetera, they're all working from the same assumptions and the same decision-making

**00:04:40–00:04:46** model. But in effect, what it means is they pretty much know what each other is doing.

**00:04:46–00:04:52** That's the key. If we can get people to not be afraid of what the others are doing,

**00:04:53–00:04:58** if they're physiotherapists, and this is a classic one, if the physiotherapists know and understand

**00:04:58–00:05:04** what this strength staff are doing, you're going to get a better result. 100%, because they're not

**00:05:04–00:05:08** going to hold back. They're not going to keep information to themselves. They're not going to

**00:05:08–00:05:14** keep opinions. When they need to say, hey, we might need to pull up, that discussion is quite

**00:05:14–00:05:20** often a challenge in a divided environment. A lot of times these days, you start to see

**00:05:20–00:05:25** a lot more integration, and there's no question, technically, particularly in Australia, we see

**00:05:25–00:05:31** this. We see a lot of graying of the zone between S&C. You've got the physiotherapists and the S&C,

**00:05:31–00:05:38** the physiotherapists quite often are hedging towards performance. Equally, there's a lot of

**00:05:38–00:05:43** S&C coaches hedging the back towards rehabilitation and doing more work in that space.

**00:05:44–00:05:51** So there's a lot of gray zone. The trust comes and the process comes when all those staff members

**00:05:51–00:05:54** start to understand what everybody else is doing, and they know what's going to happen.

**00:05:55–00:06:00** So when we hand them over, when we hand that hamstring over from day four to the running

**00:06:00–00:06:07** staff, and we've got to get moving, the physio staff know what's coming because you've already

**00:06:07–00:06:12** planned it. You're always going to have to adapt, but I think your plan is you'd made

**00:06:12–00:06:18** a starting point. So with these sort of frameworks, the best case scenario you're going to get

**00:06:18–00:06:24** is just going to be adopted and embraced, especially if all your staff have got a role in the

**00:06:24–00:06:32** development of that. However, worst, that system may only just be tolerated. In some cases,

**00:06:33–00:06:37** it may even be resisted. That's where an important distinction needs to be made.

**00:06:38–00:06:44** There's a very big difference between the technical challenge of saying, hey,

**00:06:44–00:06:48** listen, I believe there's that, there's point A and there's point B.

**00:06:49–00:06:53** I think that we need to look at point B for these reasons and making a really good

**00:06:54–00:06:58** process about it. That's great. Except that you should, as a leader, you should respect that,

**00:06:58–00:07:03** respect that point of view, examine it, and deal with it on face value. However,

**00:07:04–00:07:09** there is often, there is the occasion I have seen this, not more than once, where a staff member

**00:07:09–00:07:17** actively rebels. They actually work against the system. Now, you need to be on top of this.

**00:07:17–00:07:22** You need to be watching for this. It does occur. I saw this a couple of years ago in the AFL

**00:07:22–00:07:27** in an environment where I was working as a consultant. There was a high speed forward,

**00:07:28–00:07:33** so like a large player very fast. He'd had a history of hamstring injuries and he had a low grade

**00:07:33–00:07:40** hamstring. He'd been out for whatever it was, 14 days. He was coming back during the third week

**00:07:40–00:07:46** in that building for 21 days. The performance manager said we're working up to, let's say

**00:07:46–00:07:51** it was a third on Wednesday before a Saturday game. We'll drop the load off from there and

**00:07:51–00:07:56** we'll freshen this guy up and get him ready to play. Coaches on board, we're all on.

**00:07:56–00:08:01** But a physiotherapist in that instance, and I'm not ragging on physiotherapist, but this is just

**00:08:01–00:08:09** a duplicitous individual. This individual said in his mind, he thought they needed to test eccentric

**00:08:09–00:08:15** hamstring strength on the Friday before the game. He took the player out and no one was around,

**00:08:15–00:08:19** and he did the test and did a maximal test. Whatever, they got good numbers.

**00:08:20–00:08:26** The kid ended up tearing the next day because clearly he'd overcooked him. On the back of

**00:08:26–00:08:31** everything else that was been going on, their entire package of load, whatever that was,

**00:08:31–00:08:34** they'd added this thing in, which wasn't part of the game or part of the plan.

**00:08:35–00:08:41** The athlete got injured. Now, that's an incredibly duplicitous play, but

**00:08:42–00:08:47** you need to be cognizant that in a time when you're challenging people professionally,

**00:08:48–00:08:56** there is the possibility for that open rebellion. In that sort of framework, if you've got the

**00:08:56–00:09:01** framework and someone deliberately goes outside of it, it gives you an easy way to discuss that up

**00:09:01–00:09:06** the chain with transparency about what this person needs to go. We need to get rid of them.

**00:09:06–00:09:11** They're clearly not with us, so forth and so on. You've got a process.

**00:09:11–00:09:21** To protect your athlete, to protect the department, you need to work towards

**00:09:21–00:09:27** protecting also your integrity of decision-making and making sure that you've got a system like this

**00:09:27–00:09:31** in place and getting that framework, so getting everybody together.

**00:09:33–00:09:40** Now, beyond that, those sort of frameworks give you the opportunity to build standard

**00:09:40–00:09:44** operating procedures, which again, it's not creative bureaucracy for bureaucracy's sake,

**00:09:44–00:09:48** but it's giving you as a leader a framework from which you can work with your staff,

**00:09:48–00:09:55** which is absolutely critical because sometimes it is incredibly important to understand

**00:09:56–00:10:02** who you've got. As famously said by others, get the right people on the bus first.

**00:10:03–00:10:07** One of the most important things in business, I don't recall specifically the person who said it,

**00:10:07–00:10:13** but get the right people on the bus and then you can move forward. It's tough. It can be tough

**00:10:13–00:10:20** figuring that out. A very recent example for me, working with a larger SEC college football team in

**00:10:20–00:10:24** the US, and they're in a position where they've disappointed a whole lot of new staff, head coaches

**00:10:24–00:10:29** come, brought their performance grid with them, but much of the medical staff are remaining in

**00:10:29–00:10:36** place, and they are diametrically opposed. You've got a performance staff who are used to

**00:10:36–00:10:41** open collaborative working, getting a system in place where we know what we're doing,

**00:10:41–00:10:49** yet the medical staff were 100% against that. We don't share information. There's no accountability,

**00:10:49–00:10:57** that type of thing. At the surface, it looks pretty bad. However, that's a situation where

**00:10:57–00:11:01** those people had existed professionally in an environment where they didn't give information

**00:11:01–00:11:08** up the chain. In this particular instance, actually, the head coach has got skin in the

**00:11:08–00:11:14** game. He wants to know because that's the way he runs his operation. Making a stand to get that

**00:11:14–00:11:21** system in place, excuse me, is absolutely imperative. As a performance lead, you're going

**00:11:21–00:11:26** to have to have hard conversations. You're going to have to say, this is how we're going to do

**00:11:26–00:11:35** things. We need to get on with this. It is challenging. It is absolutely challenging, but

**00:11:35–00:11:42** I would say that from the outset, things that have worked incredibly well for me in this place

**00:11:43–00:11:47** is when you do have a group meeting, that first day you meet and you go, hey,

**00:11:48–00:11:53** hey, I'm Jason. This is what I do. This is how we're going to operate. This is what my system

**00:11:53–00:11:58** is. I've been employed to come here and do this. I haven't been employed to come here and get rid of

**00:11:58–00:12:02** people, but this is the system we're going to work to and you're going to need to work to it.

**00:12:03–00:12:08** We're going to need to, again, reframe our information and our process so everybody's

**00:12:08–00:12:15** encoded together. Again, like I said, everybody will know what steps are going on so that it's

**00:12:15–00:12:22** not a guessing game. Once you get those people aligned, you're certainly on the way towards

**00:12:22–00:12:30** being sustainable. I think I've used this example probably before, but

**00:12:33–00:12:40** bringing information to the team in advance is absolutely critical. Having stuff up front,

**00:12:40–00:12:45** and I think that idea of pre-season being able to say, this is what we're going to use,

**00:12:45–00:12:50** this is the information you will see. I got caught in a terrible situation once where

**00:12:51–00:12:56** in the AFL we were working with in an environment where our training field was,

**00:12:56–00:13:01** we were going to a new ground to play on, and it was particularly hard. I had all the data

**00:13:01–00:13:07** as to how hard, how much harder it was, and we had athletes with lower limb stress injuries,

**00:13:07–00:13:13** history. Now, at that time, we'd done some scans and some pretty new work from a

**00:13:14–00:13:21** sports science medical perspective. We were able to look at the risk of, rate the risk of

**00:13:21–00:13:27** these injuries going south under stress conditions, so high bone stress risk.

**00:13:28–00:13:34** Now, unfortunately, I presented a case study and a body of work which showed we predicted in six

**00:13:34–00:13:39** weeks if we went and did this, that we would get these injuries. But because I was presenting

**00:13:39–00:13:44** new information, it was too much. It was overload. I think this is where we come to that encoding

**00:13:44–00:13:51** piece where the data was too much, the medical staff couldn't process it, the physio staff were

**00:13:51–00:13:59** really good, they got on board, but the medical doctors couldn't say it. This is basically said,

**00:13:59–00:14:04** this is not an MRI, so we don't believe it, despite the fact that we presented

**00:14:04–00:14:12** literature and like to support it. But in that case, the coach, when facing an encoding problem,

**00:14:12–00:14:16** he deferred to the doctor. Well, doctor makes the decision, what are we going to do? Well,

**00:14:16–00:14:20** we're going to train, we're going to play there. And we did, and six weeks later, we've got a whole

**00:14:20–00:14:27** bunch of stress fractures. So that's not a point of saying how smart was I. What it is, in fact,

**00:14:27–00:14:34** is saying how wrong was I. As a technician, I probably did a good job, but as a leader,

**00:14:34–00:14:40** I didn't because I was in a position to get that information out there. So that again,

**00:14:40–00:14:47** that encoding problem where everyone sees it differently. So my staff could say, we all got

**00:14:47–00:14:52** on board, the physio's got on board, great. But then the other important pieces of that, the coach

**00:14:53–00:15:00** and the medical doctor pretty much stopped just short of calling it voodoo because they didn't

**00:15:00–00:15:06** understand it. They didn't have reference point for it. And it didn't fit into their model of

**00:15:06–00:15:13** what we should be doing. So it comes back down to that point. Everybody's going to see information,

**00:15:14–00:15:17** the same information, the same athlete, they're all going to see it different.

**00:15:18–00:15:25** It's our job as a leader to ensure we get that lined up as quickly as we can so that we can get

**00:15:25–00:15:32** people operating together. And if you take the KPI, the takeaway from this is, if you can get to the

**00:15:32–00:15:39** point where your staff understand what each other is doing, you're going to operate far, far more

**00:15:39–00:15:44** effectively. So there's your takeaway. Get everybody understanding everybody else. It does

**00:15:44–00:15:52** create empathy. And it does create an understanding. And in that case, we're in a position where

**00:15:52–00:15:57** people are more tolerant of the adaptation where we need to. We're also more tolerant of listening

**00:15:57–00:16:02** to other practitioners. So work on that encoding problem, same information, same

**00:16:02–00:16:16** athlete, and we make sure everybody can see it in the same way.

**00:08:41–00:08:46** you have similar injuries. You have ACLs, you have ankles, you have knees, all sorts of things

**00:08:46–00:08:55** go along. We're in a position where I walked in and literally saw that I wasn't accepting what

**00:08:55–00:09:01** the SNC staff were doing and I wasn't accepting what the physio staff were doing. Despite the

**00:09:01–00:09:07** fact that it wasn't really my remit at the time, I drew a line of sand and literally said,

**00:09:07–00:09:11** this is not happening. We're not doing that, and that, and that, and pointed out the errors.

**00:09:11–00:09:19** But I said to the folks, let's work together. I've walked them through everything that I was

**00:09:19–00:09:23** thinking, why the evidence for it, and this is particularly around frontal plane control,

**00:09:23–00:09:29** the pelvis and stance phase, whether in early stage rehabilitation walking, but it does pertain

**00:09:29–00:09:36** obviously as we move forward to running. But getting those folks to understand that from a

**00:09:36–00:09:42** different lens, we had a strong perspective from both camps at that time, that the issue to solve

**00:09:42–00:09:47** all this was strength. We've got to make them stronger. If they can't hold these positions,

**00:09:47–00:09:52** they can't control the frontal plane control of the pelvis. In stance phase, it's a strength

**00:09:52–00:09:58** issue. Therefore, we must lie on the floor and do more clams, so we must lean against the wall

**00:09:58–00:10:04** and do more abduction movements. I was able to clearly illustrate, simply by

**00:10:05–00:10:13** isolated isometrics in AB adduction, they are strong enough. With respect to the populations

**00:10:13–00:10:19** that they come from, they're strong enough. What we had was a motor control issue. The athlete had

**00:10:19–00:10:27** not developed the pattern post-injury to translate the center of mass across the stance phase and

**00:10:27–00:10:33** create a lot of motion. Fundamentally, they were strong enough, but the pattern

**00:10:33–00:10:38** that when their foot hit the ground, their pelvis didn't stabilize on the stance phase leg,

**00:10:38–00:10:48** as simple as that. Now, this concept was a little bit new to folks, but in order to get my environment

**00:10:48–00:10:52** squared away and people operating together, I needed to draw a line to stand. Now,

**00:10:52–00:10:58** I'm a technical guy. There is little doubt of that. So, I was in a position to do that.

**00:10:59–00:11:04** But if you expand that further, if you're in a bigger environment, there's more people,

**00:11:05–00:11:08** you have to decide whether you're going to be that technical person who can do it,

**00:11:08–00:11:15** or you need to get someone on who can. Now, it's up to you which way you go,

**00:11:15–00:11:20** but it's absolutely critical that if we walk back through all of this Module 6,

**00:11:20–00:11:27** the encoding problem, the translation problem, it's going to come down to what you know as

**00:11:27–00:11:34** a practitioner and where your strengths and weaknesses lie. So, evaluating yourself is as

**00:11:34–00:11:39** important as evaluating the group because your ability to develop a solution for the group is

**00:11:39–00:11:45** going to be predicated on what you know and what you can teach. And there's absolutely no doubt

**00:11:45–00:11:51** in my mind. I often talk about education and teaching in these type of environments. It's

**00:11:51–00:11:55** like a black room. People are in there walking around, bumping into them. They don't know what's

**00:11:55–00:12:00** going on. Leadership is about being able to turn on that lamp and look at the torch and say,

**00:12:00–00:12:05** hey, this is the way forward. This is the way we're going to go. That's what genuine leadership

**00:12:05–00:12:11** is about, in my opinion. So, if you can do that, great. If you can't, you need to make sure you

**00:12:11–00:12:16** got your people around. So, you can see that this all ties together. How are we going to construct

**00:12:17–00:12:23** our integrated operational environment? It's going to be dependent on you, your skills,

**00:12:23–00:12:27** but also the people around you because the development of that integrated system

**00:12:29–00:12:34** via both encoding and translation is going to be predicated on what you can deliver.

**00:12:35–00:12:42** So, review yourself hard, review your environment, and create a plan that is doable based on the

**00:12:42–00:12:57** resources you have at hand, be that yours or someone else's. Good luck.

# Video Lab 6E The Grey Zone: transcript

**00:00:00–00:00:22** Welcome to Module 60, The Grey Zone. Now in all performance environments, The Grey Zone exists.

**00:00:22–00:00:28** What I mean by The Grey Zone is the space that sits between medical and performance. Typically

**00:00:28–00:00:32** between our physiotherapy or physical therapy staff and your strength and conditioning or

**00:00:32–00:00:37** performance staff. This exists everywhere. And the important point here is that solving this

**00:00:37–00:00:43** is not about professional turf. It's not about eager. It's not about who has the highest status

**00:00:43–00:00:47** in the building. It's about understanding the specific operation moments where the two

**00:00:47–00:00:53** disciplines are working from different timelines, constraints, risk tolerances, and often very

**00:00:53–00:00:59** different definitions. So this is where value can be created. It's also where value can be destroyed.

**00:00:59–00:01:04** So the purpose of this module is to make that Grey Zone visible, to define it properly,

**00:01:04–00:01:09** and to give you a way of managing it with far greater authority. Because in most environments,

**00:01:09–00:01:14** problems are not that either side is incompetent. The problem is that the overlap between the two

**00:01:14–00:01:18** has not been structured. And if overlap has not been structured, then people will default

**00:01:18–00:01:24** to assumption. They assume that the other person sees the problem in the same way they do. They

**00:01:24–00:01:29** assume the other person values the same test information. They assume the other person

**00:01:29–00:01:35** understands the same risks. And very often, none of that is true. Now, the reason this Grey Zone

**00:01:35–00:01:40** is so important is because the educational backgrounds of these two groups of people

**00:01:40–00:01:45** are different, yet they have to work so closely together. And this is both a strength

**00:01:45–00:01:51** and a weakness. It's a strength because diversity of thinking, particularly in the rehabilitation

**00:01:51–00:01:56** and return to performance setting, is absolutely critical. You want these people coming at the

**00:01:56–00:02:01** athletes from slightly different angles in order to get the best result. They can absolutely

**00:02:01–00:02:06** strengthen the system. But it's a weakness when these two groups do not understand one another.

**00:02:06–00:02:10** When they don't understand the operational logic that the other person is coming from,

**00:02:10–00:02:14** then friction appears. And that friction usually appears in the moments that matter most,

**00:02:14–00:02:20** particularly around the rehab injury prevention zones. In those places, it is absolutely critical

**00:02:20–00:02:25** to get this right. So one of the first things we need to do as leaders is remove the elephant

**00:02:25–00:02:30** from the room. We need to call out the fact that these professions overlap in a vague way,

**00:02:30–00:02:34** not in a political way, but clearly. We need to say these are the areas where medical and

**00:02:34–00:02:39** performance are both involved. And these are areas where both groups may steal some ownership.

**00:02:39–00:02:44** They're also areas where, if we're not careful, confusion will emerge. Now, before we even talk

**00:02:44–00:02:49** about process, we need to talk about people. Because one of the critical features in improving

**00:02:49–00:02:53** this environment is understanding the people involved and profiling them. Now, we spoke

**00:02:53–00:02:58** in earlier modules about the knowledge behavior matrix and how critical that is to understand

**00:02:58–00:03:04** the people in your team. That same level of information and methodology can be applied here

**00:03:04–00:03:09** to understand the ability of one person to interact with the other and where maybe

**00:03:09–00:03:14** they sit on the continuum. So are they open or closed in their thinking? Are they willing to learn

**00:03:14–00:03:17** from the other discipline? Do they already have experience from the other discipline? Are they

**00:03:17–00:03:22** constructive style people, are they collaborative? Or are they big territorial and rigid? This all

**00:03:22–00:03:28** matters. Because the same structural model may work beautifully with one pair of practitioners

**00:03:28–00:03:32** but file badly in another. And a very experienced medical practitioner working with a young SNC

**00:03:32–00:03:39** coach may work. Two mid-career practitioners, roughly equal, may work. An outstanding physio

**00:03:39–00:03:44** in real time to run coaching skills is another structure again. So before we go building the

**00:03:44–00:03:49** model, we need to understand the people inside it. Because when you have one model that works,

**00:03:49–00:03:54** it might work for a period, you put different people into that same model and she ain't going

**00:03:54–00:03:59** to operate quite the same way. So once we understand the people, we need to define the

**00:03:59–00:04:04** operational logic of the department. And this is critical. The department has to have

**00:04:04–00:04:10** one operational logic, not a medical logic or a performance logic, but this is how we're going

**00:04:10–00:04:14** to do it. Because ultimately, the athlete will get stuck in the middle. There needs to be a

**00:04:14–00:04:20** alignment around how that rehab, return to athleticism pathway actually runs. That means

**00:04:20–00:04:26** we need clear decision points. We need clear definitions of phases and clear discussion

**00:04:26–00:04:31** around what we value. For example, what are the tests that we value in rehab? What are the

**00:04:31–00:04:37** things we trust or other things we don't trust? Do we value eccentric hamstring rehab? Do we

**00:04:37–00:04:42** value isometric measures? Do we value running exposure data? Do we value quality of movement

**00:04:42–00:04:46** over quantity? What clinical science are we looking at? All that needs to be discussed

**00:04:46–00:04:53** because we cannot have one discipline bringing in a biased view based on unsaid or unreliable

**00:04:53–00:04:57** information. Because this all links back to our earlier modules where we talked about

**00:04:57–00:05:03** technology stacks and getting accuracy and reliability, understanding the tolerance of

**00:05:03–00:05:08** the data we're measuring. This needs to be done because depending on the people that you have

**00:05:08–00:05:12** involved, people that get biased towards one or two things, they're going to bring that

**00:05:12–00:05:17** heart and that may overwhelm the other person in the environment. So it's absolutely critical.

**00:05:17–00:05:22** And as a department, we define it's not about what's your way or my way to our way

**00:05:22–00:05:28** and understanding it, getting it set hard in place. So before we allow measure to start

**00:05:28–00:05:34** to influence our pathway, we want to get information around it. Now, in my view, one of the simplest

**00:05:34–00:05:40** ways to manage a pathway, particularly in rehab, is to get your stages clear. For instance,

**00:05:40–00:05:44** return to function, return to run, return to play competition, that type of thing. Now,

**00:05:44–00:05:49** in a model I used for a long time, return to function was clearly the main of the medical

**00:05:49–00:05:54** practitioner. An athlete is acutely injured, both surgical and early stage of rehab. A medical

**00:05:54–00:05:58** practitioner has operational control. Now, that does not mean that the SNC coach disappears,

**00:05:58–00:06:03** far from it. The SNC coach is going to run in parallel. They're going to work on conditioning,

**00:06:03–00:06:07** strength, supporting physical quality, et cetera, et cetera. But the direction of the rehab in

**00:06:07–00:06:12** that phase is being controlled medically. Then we work up to return to run. And at

**00:06:16–00:06:22** of my SNC staff. Why? Because for introducing running, for the most part, in my case, my staff

**00:06:22–00:06:27** are trained to coach running. We're rebuilding exposure, preparing the athlete, and we need to

**00:06:27–00:06:32** get them more toward being an athlete again. Now, this is where it's going to depend on

**00:06:32–00:06:40** personality. That's a big faux pas. It's going to depend on personnel. If you have a physio

**00:06:40–00:06:45** that has exceptional skill in return to run and there are about, there's no question. You may need

**00:06:45–00:06:51** to modify that system. If you've got a young SNC coach, there's nothing I hate more than

**00:06:51–00:06:56** the notion that because you're an SNC coach, you're wearing a badge that says you understand running

**00:06:56–00:07:02** because many, many, many don't. That's critical. Making sure we've got the right people doing

**00:07:02–00:07:07** the right job, back to what we talked about, many modules ago. Get the right people on the

**00:07:07–00:07:11** bus and then make sure they're sitting in the right seats doing the right thing. One of the

**00:07:11–00:07:17** key points then is signing responsibility. You cannot leave that gray zone unowned. It has to

**00:07:17–00:07:23** be owned so that everybody contributes and everyone is accountable because if it's not,

**00:07:23–00:07:28** they'll go the other way. The person operation responsible at each point is the person who has

**00:07:28–00:07:32** to answer the questions. As a department head, if I ask where is rehabilitation at,

**00:07:32–00:07:37** I need to know who's answering. If I ask why running progression change, I need to know who

**00:07:37–00:07:43** owns that decision, I want that answer directly to me. The clarity must be essential. Now,

**00:07:43–00:07:48** in that case, from a leadership perspective, tactically, what I've done many, many times

**00:07:48–00:07:53** in the past, particularly in that return to run phase, we may have the SNC coach ultimately

**00:07:53–00:07:59** being responsible, but I'll ask questions of the physio staff because if the SNC coach

**00:07:59–00:08:03** should have explained it with clarity to the medical staff, they should be able to

**00:08:03–00:08:07** relate to me. If they can relate to me accurately, then we're in a good spot. It's a good way to

**00:08:07–00:08:13** cross-check where your operations are. Remembering that set and forget is a really bad way to run

**00:08:13–00:08:19** your department. You need to be operationally massaging it all the time to make sure that

**00:08:19–00:08:26** all the pieces are in place. Where does this lead us? We need to talk about levels of decision.

**00:08:26–00:08:30** This is where departments can get into trouble because people may know the broad phase and

**00:08:30–00:08:35** what we're doing, but they don't know what decisions they're empowered to make within that.

**00:08:35–00:08:40** Can they change the program? Can they progress loading? Can they remove an athlete from training?

**00:08:40–00:08:46** Can they reduce a field session and take somebody off? All of those things are absolutely critical

**00:08:46–00:08:51** to understand because some things are going to need to come through this department lead

**00:08:51–00:08:56** without question, but understanding where each person sits within those decision gates

**00:08:56–00:09:02** is absolutely correct. Noting in advance is critical because two things will happen if

**00:09:02–00:09:06** you don't. People will either overreach, they'll go too far, or they'll hesitate and do nothing

**00:09:06–00:09:12** and hold people back for weeks and weeks on end. If they're not in power to make a push forward,

**00:09:12–00:09:17** which comes back to your program design, in many cases, that should be guiding you on

**00:10:43–00:10:49** Now, to make the grades going clearer, getting your staff doing a walkthrough is an absolutely

**00:07:09–00:07:15** you can only speak data. So you can't say we're under pressure from the grand final to get this

**00:07:15–00:07:20** guy right, doesn't matter. Give me the facts. What can we get done by day five? What can we

**00:07:20–00:07:25** get done by day seven? What can we get done by day nine? Can we get them to the game? That type

**00:07:25–00:07:32** thing. Take all the emotion out of it. However, from my own perspective, I will quite regularly

**00:07:32–00:07:38** look in myself and say, right, we've got to think this through logically. We've got to think

**00:07:38–00:07:42** this, take the emotion out of it. I've got to think about this from another perspective.

**00:07:42–00:07:47** What does this look like from the athletes? All that type of thing. But what you're doing

**00:07:47–00:07:54** is developing a manner or a way in which you can approach problems in a more unstructured way.

**00:07:54–00:07:59** So rather than going down, as I said, the group think idea where we get everybody down

**00:07:59–00:08:04** the same path, particularly when we've got repeat problems. When you've got an issue that

**00:08:04–00:08:09** comes back and back again, so where's the problem? We haven't identified it. Now,

**00:08:09–00:08:15** I've unfortunately been in the position where over the course of time I was involved in AFL.

**00:08:16–00:08:20** We're a very, very good team. We're at top of the table, all that sort of thing. We had a run

**00:08:20–00:08:26** of stelitis injuries, all recalcitrant type things. The athlete would finish the game,

**00:08:26–00:08:31** no problem. So we're like, we won, tick it off, move on. But then by Monday, they turn up and

**00:08:31–00:08:37** go, hey, my calf's a bit sore. So we had these insidious onset tears, which were all very small,

**00:08:37–00:08:42** but they were fundamentally fatigue issues. They weren't, they didn't rupture like it's

**00:08:42–00:08:47** blood in any way, shape or form. Through the course of their game and their load,

**00:08:47–00:08:52** that's what was happening. Over and over again, we ended up going down and down the same path.

**00:08:53–00:08:58** Trying to find an answer to that, and certainly one that the coaching group at the time could

**00:08:58–00:09:03** understand or more, not understand, they could intellectually understand it. They had to

**00:09:03–00:09:09** understand it emotionally, particularly the head coach, who although very intelligent would get

**00:09:09–00:09:15** emotional about how things went. So trying to find a solution to that was an amazing process.

**00:09:15–00:09:19** What ended up happening was I had to use the doctor to go to the coach and say,

**00:09:20–00:09:26** just stop, just stop everything. Because at the time, coach wasn't listening to the

**00:09:26–00:09:33** sports science, the analytical component. It was like the doctor going in and giving the devastating

**00:09:33–00:09:39** news of, you have cancer, you have to do this. It was he walked in and just went right,

**00:09:39–00:09:45** you've got to stop, stop, do nothing. Let's take the foot off each other, which we did.

**00:09:45–00:09:48** We went really the other way. We literally stopped training for a period,

**00:09:49–00:09:55** and as that worked out, it drove us into a grand final and went from there. However,

**00:09:55–00:10:00** it was a different approach. We understood the issues, but the approach was different.

**00:10:01–00:10:07** The idea of structured thinking under pressure is about looking at different ways. Now, again,

**00:10:07–00:10:12** when you look at things like this, Daniel Kahneman's book, Thinking Fast, Thinking Slow,

**00:10:12–00:10:19** you look at the two components of how people make decisions. The fast, automatic, intuitive,

**00:10:19–00:10:26** experiential-based, quick, prone to bias type thing, that's the thing. That happens.

**00:10:27–00:10:31** Then we have the smaller, more deliberate analytical, requires effort and attention.

**00:10:31–00:10:38** They're two different things. System 2 can override the errors of System 1,

**00:10:38–00:10:46** but you've got to get past that. Again, it calls into discussion. Can we direct our thinking?

**00:10:47–00:10:51** What's something to put in front of us? Maybe the first thing that we come up with is not

**00:10:51–00:10:56** what we listen to. We need to sit back and look at the most important things,

**00:10:57–00:11:02** and look at the information. What is it? Is there something that needs more time

**00:11:02–00:11:06** to be figured out? This idea of adversarial stress testing,

**00:11:06–00:11:13** pushing ideas, pushing them, pushing yourself to find, have we exhausted everything we've got?

**00:11:13–00:11:21** I think, as a final wrap to this, if you look at the Oodaloop systems that are utilized in the

**00:11:21–00:11:27** military, it's really about orientation in the first place. There's a void in mistake by ensuring

**00:11:27–00:11:33** that we're orientating the way we're focusing in the first place. That's the first part of

**00:11:33–00:11:38** the Oodaloop. There are many ways of thinking in a structured manner, but what you need to ensure

**00:11:38–00:11:44** that is, in that pressured environment of high performance sport, that you get a chance to step

**00:11:44–00:11:50** away. You must make time. You cannot be working in the business all the time. You need to work on

**00:11:50–00:11:57** the business. As a leader, on the business component is how you address the system.

**00:11:57–00:12:06** We talked about, in the final component of Module 6, VLAB 6.8, I talked about don't let things be

**00:12:06–00:12:12** set and forget. Let's say we're building that system between the performance and medical stuff.

**00:12:12–00:12:19** Once you've built one that's working, you need to keep reassessing it. You can't just let it go

**00:12:19–00:12:23** and say, it's going to burn forever, because you're going to have different people come in

**00:12:23–00:12:27** and out of that. You might have people start to evolve their ideas. You might have a young

**00:12:27–00:12:32** practitioner in S&C enrolled in the first place, but after a year or so, he starts to develop new

**00:12:32–00:12:39** ideas. That does happen. People change. Equally, technology changes. Information changes. We get

**00:12:39–00:12:44** more information. We know more about a situation now, two years later, than we might have done

**00:12:44–00:12:50** previously. There's a lot of different moving paths. The point to all of that is ensuring

**00:12:50–00:12:57** that, as a leader, you do take a step back. You do put your time into the business, but you work

**00:12:57–00:13:02** on the business by stepping away and reviewing. Reviewing all the parts, but as a central thing,

**00:13:02–00:13:09** as crass as it may sound, answering the question, what will suck this up? What will unravel me?

**00:13:09–00:13:13** This is all working really well. What will mess it up? If you can do that,

**00:13:13–00:13:20** and whether it's by the tent man rule, or the bono's detached, or whatever it is,

**00:13:20–00:13:26** you need to come up with a methodology that ensures that you approach those problems regularly,

**00:13:26–00:13:31** because they can become problems. What seems nice and stable and everything's cool,

**00:13:31–00:13:36** at the moment, may unravel at the point when you don't need it to. Staying on top of that is a

**00:13:36–00:13:42** critical part of leadership. In any case, I recommend going to watch World War Z and

**00:13:42–00:13:47** understand that while it's a little bit dramatized, it is actually real. That's how we

**00:13:47–00:13:58** produce structured thinking under pressure.

# Podcast 6 — Structured Thinking Under Pressure: summary

Source: downloaded Podcast 6 audio, transcribed locally with faster-whisper. Timestamps refer to the media. The transcript is a machine-generated, unverified draft. Historical references and injury anecdotes are the speaker's account and have not been independently checked.

## Main idea

The speaker urges leaders to make time outside daily operations to ask what could derail a plan or expose a weakness in the department's system. A team can share a common process and still overlook an important alternative, especially under time pressure. (00:00–01:41; 03:22–04:06)

## Ways to challenge a plan

- Assign someone to argue against the group's favored explanation or proposal. The speaker uses the “tenth man” idea from *World War Z* as a memorable example of deliberate dissent. The film and historical references are illustrations here, not evidence for a particular decision method. (01:42–04:00)
- Let team members offer their perspectives before the leader speaks, then test the proposed approach with specific questions. The speaker describes a coach who listened quietly before asking where a plan might fail. (04:59–06:34)
- Deliberately switch viewpoints: examine the facts apart from the pressure surrounding a decision, then consider how it looks to the athlete and other stakeholders. The speaker connects this to Edward de Bono's “six hats” idea. (06:34–08:04)

He recounts a period of repeated calf problems in an AFL team and says the group changed course only after a doctor delivered a message the coach could accept. This is a personal account of decision dynamics; the transcript does not establish the injuries' cause or the effect of the training change. (08:04–10:00)

**Practical takeaway:** Set aside regular time to review an apparently stable system, identify what could go wrong, and revise it as staff, technology, and knowledge change. (11:13–13:58)
# Video Lab 6A — The Integration Problem: summary

Source: downloaded Lab 6A video, transcribed locally with faster-whisper. Timestamps refer to the media. The transcript is a machine-generated, unverified draft. Clinical and performance anecdotes are the speaker's account and have not been independently checked.

## Main idea

The speaker describes an integration failure: a practitioner may collect useful information, yet it does not influence decisions because the organization has no reliable way to interpret, discuss, or act on it. He asks listeners to trace a signal from collection through review to a decision and action. (00:00–01:20; 05:54–06:58)

## Five break points

1. **Language gap:** Teams use different terms or underlying models for athlete status, readiness, risk, or rehabilitation. (06:58–07:54)
2. **Decision pathway gap:** No agreed route identifies who collects, reviews, discusses, and uses technical information, including what triggers a conversation. (07:54–08:41)
3. **Authority gap:** A senior decision-maker can override a technical recommendation without discussion or explanation. The speaker favors hearing competing cases and explaining the decision. (08:41–10:20)
4. **Relationship deficit:** The person who must act does not yet understand or trust the evidence. The speaker says practitioners share responsibility for preparing colleagues to interpret new information. (10:20–12:17)
5. **Process absence:** Missing meeting gates, decision checkpoints, or review steps let a team skip important intermediate judgments. (12:17–13:14)

## Application

The speaker recommends examining a past decision to identify **which** link failed and what it cost downstream. He gives a personal account involving training surface and bone stress injuries, while acknowledging that he had not communicated his evidence in a form colleagues could use. That account illustrates his communication point; it does not establish a general injury prediction rule. (13:14–15:38)
# Video Lab 6B — The Encoding Problem: summary

Source: downloaded Lab 6B video, transcribed locally with faster-whisper. Timestamps refer to the media. The transcript is a machine-generated, unverified draft. Injury accounts and causal explanations are attributed to the speaker and have not been independently verified.

## Main idea

Different disciplines can review the same athlete and data through different priorities: rehabilitation, overall health, competition readiness, or training exposure. The speaker calls this an “encoding problem” and assigns leaders the job of aligning the terms, assumptions, and decision process across groups. (00:00–02:44)

## Proposed approach

- Write down how a case will be assessed, the checkpoints, expected timing, and who will act at each handoff. A shared plan gives the coach a clear account of current status and expected availability while leaving room for deliberate changes. The hamstring timeline in the video is an illustration, not a clinical schedule to apply generally. (02:44–04:28)
- Have medical, physiotherapy, strength, and sport science staff help build the framework and learn what each other does. The speaker sees that shared understanding as a basis for clearer handoffs and useful challenges to a plan. (04:28–06:37)
- Distinguish a reasoned technical objection from a person disregarding an agreed process. The speaker offers an anecdote about a disputed pre-game hamstring test; this transcript cannot establish why the subsequent injury occurred. (06:38–09:31)
- Explain the operating model early, especially when joining an existing department, and introduce evidence before a pressured decision. The speaker reflects on a past bone stress case where he believes he introduced unfamiliar information too late for colleagues to evaluate it. (09:33–15:18)

**Practical takeaway:** Build a shared account of the case and the steps ahead so each discipline understands the others' work, the decision points, and how to raise a concern. (15:18–16:16)
# Video Lab 6C — The Translation Problem: summary

Source: downloaded Lab 6C video, transcribed locally with faster-whisper. Timestamps refer to the media. The transcript is a machine-generated, unverified draft. Technical and clinical examples are the speaker's account, not independently validated guidance.

## Main idea

After discussing how disciplines interpret the same information differently in Lab 6B, the speaker focuses on the cost of repeatedly explaining a case to each group. He proposes early education and a shared operating framework so routine concepts and decisions need less translation during the season. (00:00–02:25)

## How he proposes closing the gap

- Repeated explanations signal that the team may not share assumptions or agreed processes. A leader can define the method directly or use workshops and staff development sessions to build it collaboratively. (02:26–03:47)
- The leader needs enough technical knowledge to teach the framework, or trusted staff who can. He asks aspiring leaders to assess which domains they can guide themselves and where they need specialist support. (03:47–05:55; 07:24–08:25)
- Align the *use* of a measure before a decision meeting: what question it answers, when it matters, and when it should not drive the case. The speaker uses eccentric hamstring data to illustrate how an unplanned measure can disrupt an agreed discussion. He says disciplinary differences remain valuable within a shared process. (05:55–07:21)

The speaker recounts challenging a team's explanation for a movement pattern after injury and teaching an alternative interpretation. That case illustrates his leadership method; the transcript alone does not establish a general diagnosis or treatment rule. (08:30–10:58)

**Practical takeaway:** Review both the team's knowledge gaps and the leader's own limits, then choose a feasible education plan with the right technical people involved. (10:59–12:57)
# Video Lab 6D — The Decision Pathway: summary

Source: downloaded Lab 6D video, transcribed locally with faster-whisper. Timestamps refer to the media. The transcript is a machine-generated, unverified draft. Examples involving athlete decisions illustrate a workflow; they are not clinical guidance.

## Main idea

The speaker asks teams to make the route from an observation to an action explicit, including who owns each step. He describes six stages: **data capture → quality control → analysis → interpretation → communication → decision and action**. (00:00–02:02)

## Five gaps to audit

1. **Dirty data, between capture and quality control.** Check that a collection protocol was followed and that anomalies are caught before data enters reports or a long-term database. Name an owner for this check. (02:02–02:59)
2. **Expertise, between quality control and analysis.** A reliable measurement can still be evaluated against an unsuitable threshold or without its normal context. Ask who sets and reviews the thresholds, including software defaults. (02:59–04:24)
3. **Interpretation, between analysis and meaning.** A number may reach a meeting without anyone saying what it means for the athlete or the decision. Excess data can also exceed the team's capacity to interpret it. (04:24–05:32)
4. **Communication, between interpretation and decision-maker.** Technical language can obscure the requested action. The speaker recommends leading with a clear recommendation and supplying supporting detail in a form the recipient can use. (05:32–08:54)
5. **Authority, between recommendation and action.** Even a clear recommendation may be ignored if no formal decision gate or override process exists. The speaker calls for explicit decision authority and a record of recommendations and decisions. (08:54–10:50)

**Practical takeaway:** Trace a recent important decision through all six stages, identify the gap that most affects decisions, and assign a concrete owner and process to close it. (10:52–12:11)
# Video Lab 6E — The Grey Zone: summary

Source: downloaded Lab 6E video, transcribed locally with faster-whisper. Timestamps refer to the media. The transcript is a machine-generated, unverified draft. The return-to-activity phases are the speaker's example of team organization, not a patient-specific protocol.

## Main idea

The speaker calls the overlap between medical or physiotherapy staff and strength and performance staff the “grey zone.” He argues that differences in training, priorities, timelines, and risk tolerance become a problem when the overlap has no agreed operating rules. The leader's task is to make responsibilities and decisions explicit while preserving each discipline's perspective. (00:00–02:44)

## Organizing the overlap

- Consider the actual practitioners' skills and willingness to collaborate before assigning roles. A job title alone does not establish who is best equipped for a specific task. (02:44–03:59; 06:33–07:11)
- Agree on the phases, decision points, measures, and criteria the department will use. The speaker describes one model with medical leadership early in rehabilitation and strength staff taking operational responsibility for return to running, while both continue to contribute. He says this division should change when personnel skills warrant it. (03:59–07:11)
- Name an operational owner for each phase, define what that person can change independently, and state which decisions require escalation. Also specify who must be informed and how quickly when an athlete's plan changes. (07:11–10:43)

## Team exercise

Walk through one rehabilitation case twice: once from the physiotherapist's priorities and constraints, and once from the strength coach's. Compare the accounts at each handoff, then agree on ownership, progression criteria, information to transfer, change authority, and notification rules. (10:43–13:02)

**Practical takeaway:** Make the shared work visible and assign responsibility at each transition so the athlete's plan can pass between disciplines without relying on assumptions. (12:12–13:02)

4. **Communication, between interpretation and decision-maker.** Technical language can obscure the requested action. The speaker recommends leading with a clear recommendation and supplying supporting detail in a form the recipient can use. (05:32–08:54)
5. **Authority, between recommendation and action.** Even a clear recommendation may be ignored if no formal decision gate or override process exists. The speaker calls for explicit decision authority and a record of recommendations and decisions. (08:54–10:50)

**Practical takeaway:** Trace a recent important decision through all six stages, identify the gap that most affects decisions, and assign a concrete owner and process to close it. (10:52–12:11)

Walk through one rehabilitation case twice: once from the physiotherapist's priorities and constraints, and once from the strength coach's. Compare the accounts at each handoff, then agree on ownership, progression criteria, information to transfer, change authority, and notification rules. (10:43–13:02)
