# Module 4: The Integration Problem (Data to Decisions)

Note on numbering: the course materials label this block internally as "Module 6" (Section 1 / 6A, 6B Part A and Part B, 6C or 6D, 6E, Podcast 6). The lecturer is Dr Jason Weber (Old Bull Performance). The folder in Eric's Drive calls it Module 4, and that is the number used here. Where the video says "Module 6C" it is the file titled 6D The Decision Pathway; where it says "6B Part 2" it is 6C The Translation Problem.

The module's argument is that technically strong practitioners fail to influence decisions not because they lack knowledge but because the department has no operating model that carries information from collection to action. Weber names five places where that chain breaks (language, decision pathway, authority, relationship, process), then goes deeper on two of them: the encoding problem (each discipline reads the same athlete through a different lens) and the translation problem (someone is permanently re-explaining the basics, which is a leadership failure disguised as a communication chore). He then makes the pathway itself explicit as six stages with five audit points, and applies the whole thing to the physio to strength-and-conditioning overlap he calls the grey zone, which must be profiled, owned, gated and communicated rather than left to personality. The closing podcast and its reference document argue that once a department is aligned, the new risk is groupthink, so leaders need structured dissent (10th Man, pre-mortem, red team, OODA reorientation) built into the decision log. The through-line is Weber's own confession: he had the right data on bone stress risk and the injuries he predicted happened anyway, because he had not made the information consumable to the doctor and the coach in advance.

## Lessons

### Video Lab 6A: The Integration Problem (15:42) with Video_Lab_6A_Summary PDF, Integration Cheat Sheet PDF, Integration Problem Workbook PDF

- The failure mode: a practitioner who is "data literate" (transcript renders it "dilutriate") and analytically sharp, whose recommendations are ignored, diluted, overwritten or simply not understood. Weber has seen it across sports and countries; "it's typically not a knowledge problem, it's an integration problem" (00:01:00).
- Warning signs: no structured pathway for information to move upward; other departments do not understand what you are saying; junior staff who do not know they are stage one of a five-stage process; terminology confusion between and within departments; a dismissive owner of a "domain"; and philosophical differences in models of performance, rehabilitation, monitoring or decision-making (00:01:20 to 00:04:22).
- Cost of no shared framework: the Italian analogy (think in English, speak Italian, hear Italian, convert back) as a description of the daily cognitive load of translating across disciplines (00:05:25).
- Four self-audit questions (00:05:54): when did your data last change a major decision; can you trace collection to action; how many people can explain the monitoring system; how many could explain the return-to-run model.
- Five integration breakpoints (00:06:58 to 00:13:07), confirmed word for word in the Cheat Sheet and the 6A Summary PDF. Authority gradient gets the most nuance: someone has to make the call, but there should always be an explanation, delivered in the meeting and again privately afterwards, and a good leader lets the argument run rather than shutting it down (00:08:41 to 00:10:20).
- The Cheat Sheet adds a diagnostic line not in the video: "If your recommendation changes as it moves up the chain, there is likely an integration leak" (p.1).

### Video Lab 6B: The Encoding Problem (16:23) with Module_6B_Part_A PDF

- Different disciplines encode the same facts differently: physiotherapy sees tissue tolerance and adaptation; medical sees overall health and risk; strength staff see outputs and readiness; sport science sees load and exposure; the coach sees availability (can they train, can they play). Nobody disagrees on the facts; they disagree on what the facts mean (00:00:23 to 00:01:28; PDF p.1).
- Realigning the encoding framework is "the core job of someone in a leadership position" and takes time, discipline and a written process: "when we get A, this is what we do" (00:01:46 to 00:02:25; PDF p.1).
- Worked example: a grade 2A biceps femoris hamstring should already have an agreed assessment, checkpoints, tempo, day-by-day expectations and a realistic return-to-performance timeline before it happens. The same model can be applied to performance progressions, not just rehab (00:03:01 to 00:03:45).
- The health indicator of an aligned system: staff know what each other are doing, so the physio is not afraid of what the strength coach will do on day four and does not withhold opinions (00:04:46 to 00:06:07).
- Technical challenge versus active resistance: a reasoned objection should be respected and examined; a staff member who works outside the agreed process (the physio who ran an unplanned maximal eccentric hamstring test the day before a game, after which the player tore) is a different problem, and the written framework is what lets you take that up the chain transparently (00:06:38 to 00:09:31; PDF p.2).
- Standard operating procedures are not bureaucracy; they are the tool for finding out who can operate inside a collaborative system. "Get the right people on the bus." The SEC football example (new performance staff who share everything meeting incumbent medical staff who share nothing) and the first-meeting script: "I'm Jason, this is what I do, this is how we're going to operate" (00:09:33 to 00:12:22; PDF p.2).
- Weber's confession: bone stress risk data was rejected by the doctor as "not an MRI", the coach deferred to the doctor, and the predicted injuries arrived six weeks later. "As a technician I probably did a good job, but as a leader I didn't" (00:12:33 to 00:15:18; PDF p.2).

### Video Lab 6C: The Translation Problem (13:04) with Module_6B_Part_B PDF

- Translation is the downstream cost of unresolved encoding: explaining the same issue to medical, then strength, then physio, then the coach, every day. It is a "performance leak inside the organisation" (PDF p.1) and a threat to a leader's "cognitive survivability" (00:07:24).
- Principle: discipline equals freedom. "Avoid translation, focus on education, and focus on it early" (00:02:25). Some explanation is inevitable, especially executive-level updates for the coach, but constant re-explanation is diagnostic information that the system is not aligned (00:02:47 to 00:03:04).
- Two routes to fix it: draw a line in the sand ("this is how we operate"), which is fast but creates friction; or build alignment through workshops and internal CPD, which takes longer but brings people in rather than pushing on them (00:03:04 to 00:03:41; PDF p.1 to p.2).
- The leader's choice, Option A or Option B: either you have the technical depth to explain the framework yourself (the "rawest form of leadership") or you hire and trust the person who can. Not every great leader is a great technician and vice versa; a physio promoted to lead a department must be honest about who will own the running and speed programme (00:04:03 to 00:05:55; 00:07:55 to 00:08:25; PDF p.2).
- Fashionable or divisive metrics (the eccentric hamstring test is the example) must have an agreed place in the framework before a high-level meeting, so old debates do not re-open when someone "brings up data we've already said we're not going to use in this situation" (00:06:12 to 00:07:21; PDF p.2).
- Worked example: a multi-sport environment where both physio and strength staff framed poor frontal-plane pelvic control in stance as a strength deficit (more clams, more wall abduction). Weber showed with isolated isometric abduction that athletes were already strong enough and reframed it as a motor control problem. The point is a line in the sand drawn with evidence and education rather than authority (00:08:30 to 00:10:58; PDF p.2 to p.3).

### Video Lab 6D: The Decision Pathway (12:14) (no companion PDF)

- Every significant decision (return to play, load adjustment, programme modification) travels the same six stages: data capture, quality control, analysis, interpretation, communication, decision and action (00:01:06 to 00:02:02).
- Five failure points sit between stages, each with an audit question (00:02:02 to 00:10:50). Detail in the Frameworks section below.
- The communication gap example: "moderate signal that readiness might be compromised, want to be cautious" lands with a coach as "uncertain, no recommendation", when the practitioner actually meant "reduce intensity 15%". Neither side is wrong; the message was operationally opaque (00:06:27 to 00:06:59).
- The 20-second rule: if you are more than 20 seconds from a recommendation, the coach has stopped listening. Lead with the recommendation, not the method or the number (00:07:46 to 00:08:48).
- Weber guards the channel between his level and the head coach; a junior sport scientist "gibbering" to the head coach is fine once or twice for development, then it is a risk (00:07:08 to 00:07:34).
- Authority gap example: physio recommends no contact, coach agrees, 20 minutes later the athlete is in full contact with no recorded override. Keep strong written notes on recommendations and decisions so "don't come back and blame it on me" holds (00:09:11 to 00:10:34). Across 30 years the highest-friction failure point is usually the one closest to stage six, because that is where consequences are visible (00:11:09).

### Video Lab 6E: The Grey Zone (13:15) with Grey Zone Workbook PDF and Grey Zone Summary PDF

- The grey zone is the space between medical (physio) and performance (strength and conditioning) where both work on the same athlete from different timelines, risk tolerances and definitions. It exists everywhere; the problem is that it has not been structured, so people default to assumption (00:00:22 to 00:01:35; Summary p.1).
- People before process: profile every person in the interface on the Knowledge-Behaviour Matrix (from Lab 1b) because the same model works with one physio-S&C pair and fails with another (00:02:44 to 00:03:59; Summary p.2).
- One operational logic, not a medical logic running alongside a performance logic: agree phase definitions, which tests you trust, which data need triangulation, and what "athlete ready" means before measurement starts influencing the pathway (00:03:59 to 00:05:28; Summary p.3).
- Weber's reference model: medical owns return to function, S&C owns return to run (unless an exceptional running physio changes the calculus), return to play is shared by pre-agreed criteria, and return to competition is department-lead sign-off. "Wearing the S&C badge" does not mean you can coach running (00:05:34 to 00:07:11; Summary p.4).
- Ownership, empowerment and communication: every phase has one operationally responsible person who answers when the lead asks; every decision type has an explicit act-or-escalate level; every decision event has a pre-defined notification list and speed. Set and forget is how departments divide (00:07:11 to 00:10:43).
- The walkthrough exercise: tell one case twice, physio's eyes then S&C's eyes, find where the logics diverge, and write an integration protocol for each divergence (00:10:43 to 00:12:12).

### Podcast 6: Structured Thinking Under Pressure (14:04) with Structured_Thinking_Under_Pressure PDF

- "Seeing around corners" is what separates leaders; you can only do it by stepping out of the processes you built (working on the business, not in it) and asking "what could derail this?" A trusted associate once asked Weber, bluntly, what could mess the plan up, and that question is the whole method (00:00:41 to 00:02:02).
- The 10th Man Rule from World War Z is dramatised but real: Israel's Devil's Advocate Unit was created after the 1973 Yom Kippur intelligence failure. Once you have everyone "playing nicely in the sandpit" (which the rest of the course pushes you toward), groupthink becomes the new risk (00:02:02 to 00:04:37; PDF p.1 to p.2).
- Young practitioners treat current technology as measuring what it claims to; most of it infers an outcome (the athlete can run, the athlete has recovered). Do not let the group agree its way past that (00:04:06 to 00:04:37).
- Two meeting techniques: the international rugby coach who sits silent, lets every perspective land, then asks questions designed to unravel the plan ("if I can unravel it, it will unravel when we deploy it"); and Weber's own habit of turning one staff member against another to see what survives (00:05:04 to 00:06:34).
- De Bono's Six Hats in practice: "for the next five minutes you can only speak data. Not 'we're under pressure for the grand final'. What can we get done by day five, day seven, day nine?" (00:06:34 to 00:07:32).
- Kahneman's System 1 and 2, adversarial stress testing, and OODA's orientation stage all say the same thing: the first answer is not necessarily the one to act on, and a system that works today must be re-reviewed as staff, technology and knowledge change (00:10:01 to 00:13:42).
- The AFL calf case: recurrent insidious-onset fatigue tears in a top-of-table team that the coach could understand intellectually but not emotionally; the fix was getting the doctor to walk in and say "stop everything", a different messenger for the same conclusion (00:08:04 to 00:10:00).

## Frameworks and tools taught

### 1. The Five Integration Breakpoints (6A; Cheat Sheet p.1; Workbook p.4; 6A Summary p.1)

Use as a diagnostic on any past decision where good technical work did not change the outcome. Tick which one (or which combination) broke:

1. Language gap: no shared framework for describing athlete status, readiness or risk. Includes philosophical gaps, where people understand the words but hold different models.
2. Decision pathway gap: no pre-agreed route for who collects, who reviews, where it goes next, what triggers a conversation, and where it plugs into a meeting.
3. Authority gradient: a senior figure overrides sound technical input without challenge or explanation. The fix is not to remove authority but to make overrides transparent and explained.
4. Relationship deficit: the decision maker does not trust, understand or value the source. Weber treats this as a system failure and largely the practitioner's own responsibility to pre-educate.
5. Process absence: no meeting, gate or checkpoint requires the technical input to be addressed before the decision is finalised, so the team jumps from A to X.

Product: a named breakpoint for a specific case, plus (Workbook D3) the one thing that would have needed to be different.

### 2. The Three Diagnostic Questions (Workbook p.2; video adds a fourth)

Ask of yourself or each staff member:

1. When did your data last directly change a coaching decision? If you cannot name one in the last three months, that is the answer. Then trace the pathway from collection to that decision.
2. How many people in the department could accurately explain what the monitoring system measures and why? Estimate the number, name the gaps by role and person, and state what the gap costs (data collected but unused, recommendations rejected because misunderstood).
3. What happens to your recommendations when you are not in the room? Hold, get modified, or disappear, and what determines that.
4. (Video only, 00:06:12) How many could explain the return-to-run model and its decision gates?

Product: a written statement of whether technical work is influencing outcomes or being generated and lost.

### 3. The Real-World Failure Case reflection (Integration Workbook sections A to E, p.1 to p.5)

Step by step: A1 define the integration problem in your own words as it appears in your environment; A2 rate frequency (rarely / occasionally / regularly / almost always) and describe one observable signal. C1 to C4 pick one case where the technical quality was sound but the decision process produced a poor outcome: context and who was involved; what the data indicated; what was decided instead and what overrode it; downstream cost to athlete, team, credibility, department. C5 optional table for multiple cases (Situation / What the data said / What happened instead / Downstream cost). D1 locate the break against the five breakpoints; D2 one-off or recurring, and what has prevented resolution; D3 what would have needed to be different (a process, relationship, language, structure or moment in the pathway). E complete: "The one integration failure in my current environment that I most need to resolve is..." and bring it to the live session. The workbook says the rest of the module is built as responses to this case.

### 4. The Encoding Realignment: scenario pre-commitment (6B; Part A PDF p.1)

How to run it with staff: pick a common presentation (Weber uses a grade 2A hamstring). Before it happens, write down, with every discipline in the room: how it will be assessed; the checkpoints; the tempo and day-by-day expectations (day three, four, five); the realistic return-to-performance timeline; who acts at each handover (for example day-four handover to running staff); and the criteria for adapting off the plan. The output is a document the whole staff helped build, which is what the coach sees ("this is the plan, these are the checkpoints"), and which becomes the reference for deciding whether a deviation is a reasoned technical challenge or someone working outside the system. Repeat for performance progressions, not only injuries. Health check: can the physio describe what the strength coach will do next week, and vice versa.

### 5. First-meeting operating statement and SOP stance (6B 00:11:43 to 00:12:22; Part A PDF p.2)

When inheriting a department, the first group meeting is where the encoding framework is set: who you are, what you do, how the department will operate, that you were hired to install a system and not to remove people, and that everyone will work to it. SOPs follow, and are explicitly positioned as the way to find out who can work inside a collaborative system, and the transparent basis for escalating anyone who cannot.

### 6. The Translation Audit and the Option A / Option B leadership choice (6C; Part B PDF p.1 to p.2)

Step 1: list every concept you find yourself re-explaining to a second and third audience in the same week. Each is a gap. Step 2: for each gap choose the route: line in the sand (define how we operate, accept friction) or education (workshops, internal CPD, bring people into the process). Step 3: decide honestly who will teach it. Option A: you have the technical depth, so you stand up and explain the framework. Option B: you do not, so you hire or empower the person who does and you trust them; do not defer to someone just because it is easy. Step 4: agree in advance how contested metrics (eccentric hamstring, isometrics, GPS thresholds) are framed in this environment, so they cannot re-open debates in high-level meetings. Product: an education plan sized to the resources you actually have.

### 7. The Six-Stage Decision Pathway and Five-Point Audit (6D, transcript only)

Stages: (1) data capture: GPS, force plate, RPE, clinical assessment, direct observation; (2) quality control: was the protocol followed, were conditions consistent, any anomalies; (3) analysis: thresholds, baselines; (4) interpretation: this number means the athlete is in this state; (5) communication: presenting the interpretation to the person who will act; (6) decision and action: training modified, load adjusted, athlete held.

Failure points and the audit question for each:

1. Dirty data (between 1 and 2). Unit not worn correctly, force plate not zeroed, protocol not followed, nobody caught it, and it sits in the database for six to eight weeks. Ask: who owns quality control, and what does the check specifically consist of? If the answer is "nobody, it's informal", that is the finding.
2. Expertise gap (between 2 and 3). Data are reliable but the analyst lacks the framework: normal-limit changes flagged as severe, a 50 ms RFD change on shoulder external rotation treated as an emergency. Ask: who set the thresholds, where were the defaults inherited from, is it written in a software platform, who reviews it, and is there a high-clarity handover when staff change?
3. Interpretation gap (between 3 and 4). A number is reported and the meeting moves on; nobody says what it means. Often caused by collecting more data than the system can process. Ask: when data are presented, does it stop at the number, and who is there to handle it?
4. Communication gap (between 4 and 5). Technically precise, operationally opaque, too verbose. Ask: what do you lead with, the methodology, the number or the recommendation? Apply the 20-second rule and a pre-built delivery structure for the coach ("bang, this is it, boom, boom, boom").
5. Authority gap (between 5 and 6). Clear recommendation, no decision gate, so it never becomes a decision. Ask: is there a pre-agreed process that requires technical input to be formally addressed before a high-stakes decision (return to play, selection) is finalised? If not, recommendations are "advisory at best, optional at worst".

Product: name the single failure point costing the most decision quality each week (not the one that implicates someone) and fix that first. Keep written notes on every recommendation and decision.

### 8. The Grey Zone build: seven-step protocol (6E; Grey Zone Workbook p.1 to p.12; Grey Zone Summary p.2 to p.7)

Run in this order; the workbook says the diagnostic leads into the design, which leads into the operating protocols.

Step 1, People Profile (Workbook p.2 to p.3). Map every staff member in the physio-S&C interface: Knowledge level (Handbrake: low knowledge, defaults to assumption, needs close supervision; Pawn: has knowledge but relies on instruction, hesitates at transitions; Practitioner: competent in own domain, collaboration depends on openness; Operator: high knowledge, autonomous, check for territorial bias) crossed with Behaviour (Misaligned: works against departmental logic; Coaster: present but passive, avoids calls under pressure; Catalyst: drives collaboration, anchor your protocols to this person; Beacon: sets the standard, amplifies the model or, if misaligned, undermines it). Then check combinations. Need extra structure: Misaligned x Operator; Beacon (Misaligned) x any Handbrake; two Practitioners with different domain biases; Pawn S&C + Operator Physio (physio runs rehab outside mandate). Can self-organise: Beacon x Catalyst; Operator x Operator with explicit handover points; Catalyst x Practitioner. Write: biggest risk in this specific pairing and the level of structure it needs.

Step 2, One Operational Logic (Workbook p.4; Summary p.3). Facilitate agreement, and record the agreed position not individual opinions, on six domains: hamstring rehab markers (eccentric strength, isometrics, running exposure); running readiness criteria (quality of movement versus quantity of exposure); return to full training threshold (what tests, who signs off); data we trust in-house (GPS, force plate, clinical assessment, gait analysis); data we do not act on in isolation (tools that need triangulation); and what "athlete ready" means. Leave a row blank if unresolved; the blank is the priority.

Step 3, Rehab Phase Ownership Map (Workbook p.5; Summary p.4). For Return to Function (acute / post-surgical), Return to Run (loading), Return to Play (performance rebuild), Return to Competition: who owns it, who contributes, transition criteria, escalation required. Weber's reference: medical/physio owns RTF with S&C running parallel conditioning ("physio controls direction, S&C does not wait"); S&C owns RTR in most environments; RTP is shared per pre-agreed criteria; RTC is department-lead sign-off with immediate communication to the head coach. Modify for the actual people. Pre-agree before any athlete is injured.

Step 4, Cross-Check Method (6E 00:07:43 to 00:08:13; Summary p.4). Even when S&C owns the phase, ask the physio to account for it. If S&C communicated clearly, the physio can relay the rationale; if not, the communication has not happened. This is how you verify the model is running rather than assumed.

Step 5, Decision Empowerment Checklist (Workbook p.6; Summary p.5). For each of seven decision types (progress loading within agreed programme; regress loading; remove athlete from a field session; modify a published session; progress to next rehab phase; seek external specialist referral; return athlete to full contact training) mark Yes/No for physio can act, S&C can act, must escalate to department lead. Two failure modes if you skip this: overreach (usually Operator knowledge without role boundaries) and paralysis (usually Pawn behaviour in a Practitioner role, holding athletes back for weeks waiting for permission never withheld).

Step 6, Communication Protocol (Workbook p.7; Summary p.5 to p.6). For each decision event (athlete removed from field session; rehab phase progressed; rehab phase regressed or paused; specialist referral required; return to full training cleared) fill in who is told, how fast, via what channel. Rules: the operationally responsible person owns the communication, not a bystander; the list is pre-defined per decision type; anything touching field presence is immediate, not end of session, not email; escalation triggers are pre-agreed so escalation is never a surprise. Then write the single biggest communication failure point and the one protocol change that fixes it.

Step 7, Walkthrough Exercise (Workbook p.8 to p.9; Summary p.6 to p.7). Choose one real or well-built hypothetical case. Have the physio and the S&C coach each answer, in front of each other: what does progress look like; what are the key risks right now; what data do you trust; what are your time constraints; where do you need the other discipline most; what would cause you to pause or regress. Mark the two or three divergence points where the logics conflict. For the highest-priority divergence write the integration protocol: who owns this moment; what criteria determine the outcome; what information is handed over and to whom; who can change the programme; who must be informed; what goes to the department lead without exception.

Finish with the Grey Zone Master Checklist (Workbook p.10 to p.11): 22 boxes across People Diagnosis, Operational Logic, Phase Ownership, Decision Empowerment, Communication, Ongoing Operations. "A blank box is a structural risk." Re-run after any staff change or mid-season.

### 9. Structured dissent toolkit (Podcast 6; Structured Thinking PDF p.1 to p.8)

- 10th Man Rule: when consensus forms, one person has the formal, protected obligation to argue the opposite. In OBP terms: designate that voice in the Kaigi decision log before RTR or programme calls are logged (PDF p.6).
- Six Thinking Hats (de Bono): White facts only; Red gut feel without justification; Black what could go wrong (the 10th Man hat); Yellow best case; Green alternative paths, a staged return not yet designed; Blue process control, who owns the decision and what is the review trigger. Everyone wears the same hat at the same time (parallel thinking), which removes the conflict and keeps the thinking (PDF p.2 to p.3). Weber's lightweight version: "five minutes, data only".
- Pre-Mortem (Klein / Kahneman), three steps: state the decision; project forward ("it is four weeks from now, he is re-injured, what happened?") with each person writing independently before discussion; collect and group the failure scenarios and use the most credible to add contingencies before committing (PDF p.3).
- System 1 / System 2: the Go/No-Go framework and Kaigi structure exist to force slow thinking onto decisions staff would otherwise make on pattern recognition, especially when a situation looks familiar but is not (PDF p.4).
- Red Teaming, five questions for performance decisions: under what conditions does this monitoring system give false confidence; what would have to be true about this athlete for our RTR assessment to be wrong; where are we relying on a single source; what are we not measuring and does the decision assume it is fine; if a different department looked at this data what would they conclude. Inter-departmental version: medical reviews performance decisions, S&C stress-tests medical thresholds (PDF p.4 to p.6).
- OODA loop: orientation (your mental model, the department's "concept") is the underrated failure stage; accurate data through a stale filter still produces a wrong decision. Audit the concept regularly: when did we last reorient our monitoring assumptions (PDF p.5 to p.6).

2. Translation gap identification: the 6C video (00:02:31) refers to "the workbook associated with this lab" for finding gaps where key ideas are explained constantly. Instruction: complete the People Profile before building any model; design for the real environment not the ideal; revisit after any staff change.
5. Structured Thinking: watch World War Z as a priming device (podcast 00:13:36; PDF p.6), then run the four-layer Bias Prompt Analysis on a live return-to-play or programme decision and record the review triggers in the decision log. The PDF closes with: what is your department's current concept, when did you last audit it, and how old is the filter you run monitoring data through (p.8).

# Module 4: The Integration Problem (Data to Decisions)

Numbering note: the course materials label this block internally as "Module 6" (Section 1 / 6A, 6B Part A and B, 6E, Podcast 6). The lecturer is Dr Jason Weber (Old Bull Performance). Eric's Drive folder calls it Module 4 and that number is used here. Where the video says "Module 6C" it is the file titled 6D The Decision Pathway; where it says "6B Part 2" it is 6C The Translation Problem.

The module's argument is that technically strong practitioners fail to influence decisions not because they lack knowledge but because the department has no operating model that carries information from collection to action. Weber names five places where that chain breaks (language, decision pathway, authority, relationship, process), then goes deeper on two of them: the encoding problem (each discipline reads the same athlete through a different lens) and the translation problem (someone is permanently re-explaining the basics, which is a leadership failure disguised as a communication chore). He then makes the pathway explicit as six stages with five audit points, and applies the whole thing to the physio to strength-and-conditioning overlap he calls the grey zone, which must be profiled, owned, gated and communicated rather than left to personality. The closing podcast argues that once a department is aligned, the new risk is groupthink, so leaders need structured dissent built into the decision log. The through-line is Weber's own confession: he had the right data on bone stress risk and the injuries he predicted happened anyway, because he had not made the information consumable to the doctor and the coach in advance.

## Lessons

### Video Lab 6A: The Integration Problem (15:42), with 6A Summary PDF, Integration Cheat Sheet PDF, Integration Problem Workbook PDF

- The failure mode: a data-literate, analytically sharp practitioner whose recommendations are ignored, diluted, overwritten or not understood. "It's typically not a knowledge problem, it's an integration problem" (00:01:00).
- Warning signs (00:01:20 to 00:04:22): no upward pathway; other departments do not understand you; junior staff who do not know they are stage one of a five-stage process; terminology confusion; a dismissive domain owner; philosophical differences in models of rehab, monitoring or decision-making.
- Four self-audit questions (00:05:54) and five integration breakpoints (00:06:58 to 00:13:07); see Frameworks 1 and 2.
- On authority: someone has to make the call, but always explain it, in the meeting and again privately afterwards, and let the argument run rather than shutting it down (00:08:41 to 00:10:20).
- Weber's confession: bone stress data was not "medically friendly", the coach asked what the doctor said, the doctor did not know, and the predicted injuries arrived six weeks later. "It's not just about what I can do. It's about what I can get my team to do" (00:11:59 to 00:15:10).

### Video Lab 6B: The Encoding Problem (16:23), with Module_6B_Part_A PDF

- Disciplines encode the same facts differently: physio sees tissue tolerance, medical sees health risk, strength staff see outputs, sport science sees load, the coach sees availability. Nobody disagrees on the facts; they disagree on what they mean (00:00:23 to 00:01:28; PDF p.1).
- Realigning the encoding framework is the core leadership job and requires written scenario pre-commitment: "when we get A, this is what we do" (00:01:46 to 00:03:45); see Framework 4.
- The health indicator of an aligned system is that staff know what each other will do next, so nobody withholds an opinion or a handover (00:04:46 to 00:06:07; PDF p.1).
- Reasoned technical challenge is welcome; working outside the agreed process is not. The physio who ran an unplanned maximal eccentric hamstring test the day before a game, after which the player tore, is the cautionary case, and the written framework is what lets you escalate it transparently (00:06:38 to 00:09:31; PDF p.2).
- SOPs are how you find out who can operate inside a collaborative system; the SEC football example and the first-meeting script are the model for inheriting a divided department (00:09:33 to 00:12:22; PDF p.2); see Framework 5.
- "As a technician I probably did a good job, but as a leader I didn't" (00:14:27): the doctor called the bone stress data "not an MRI", the coach deferred to the doctor.

### Video Lab 6C: The Translation Problem (13:04), with Module_6B_Part_B PDF

- Translation is the daily cost of unresolved encoding: explaining the same issue to medical, strength, physio, then coach. It is a "performance leak" (PDF p.1) and a threat to a leader's "cognitive survivability" (00:07:24).
- Discipline equals freedom: "Avoid translation, focus on education, and focus on it early" (00:02:25). Constant re-explanation is diagnostic information that the system is not aligned (PDF p.1).
- Two routes: line in the sand (fast, friction) or workshops and internal CPD (slower, brings people in) (00:03:04 to 00:03:41); and the Option A / Option B leadership choice; see Framework 6.
- Contested metrics (eccentric hamstring is the example) need an agreed place in the framework before high-level meetings so old debates cannot re-open (00:06:12 to 00:07:21; PDF p.2).
- Worked case: staff framed poor frontal-plane pelvic control in stance as a strength deficit; isolated isometric abduction showed athletes were strong enough and the problem was motor control. A line in the sand drawn with evidence and education, not authority (00:08:30 to 00:10:58; PDF p.2 to p.3).

### Video Lab 6D: The Decision Pathway (12:14), no companion PDF

- Every significant decision travels six stages: data capture, quality control, analysis, interpretation, communication, decision and action (00:01:06 to 00:02:02); five failure points sit between them, each with an audit question; see Framework 7.
- Communication example: "moderate signal, want to be cautious" lands with a coach as "uncertain, no recommendation", when the practitioner meant "reduce intensity 15%" (00:06:27 to 00:06:59).
- The 20-second rule: lead with the recommendation, not the method or the number (00:07:46 to 00:08:48). Weber guards the channel between his level and the head coach (00:07:08).
- Authority example: physio recommends no contact, coach agrees, 20 minutes later the athlete is in full contact with no recorded override. Keep written notes on recommendations and decisions (00:09:11 to 00:10:34).
- The highest-friction failure point is usually the one closest to stage six because that is where consequences are visible (00:11:09).

### Video Lab 6E: The Grey Zone (13:15), with Grey Zone Workbook PDF and Grey Zone Summary PDF

- The grey zone is where physio and strength staff work on the same athlete from different timelines, risk tolerances and definitions. It exists everywhere; the problem is it has not been structured, so people default to assumption (00:00:22 to 00:01:35; Summary p.1).
- People before process: profile everyone in the interface on the Knowledge-Behaviour Matrix, because the same model works with one pair and fails with another (00:02:44 to 00:03:59; Summary p.2).
- One operational logic, not medical and performance logics in parallel: agree phases, trusted tests, triangulation rules and what "athlete ready" means before measurement influences the pathway (00:03:59 to 00:05:28; Summary p.3).
- Weber's reference ownership model (medical owns return to function, S&C owns return to run, RTP shared, RTC department-lead sign-off) plus empowerment levels and communication rules; "wearing the S&C badge" does not mean you can coach running (00:05:34 to 00:10:43; Summary p.4 to p.6); see Framework 8.
- The walkthrough exercise: tell one case twice, physio's eyes then S&C's, find the divergence points, write an integration protocol for each (00:10:43 to 00:12:12).

### Podcast 6: Structured Thinking Under Pressure (14:04), with Structured_Thinking_Under_Pressure PDF

- "Seeing around corners" requires stepping out of the processes you built (working on the business, not in it) and asking, bluntly, what could derail this (00:00:41 to 00:02:02).
- The 10th Man Rule from World War Z is dramatised but real (Israel's Devil's Advocate Unit, post-1973). Once everyone is "playing nicely in the sandpit", groupthink is the new risk (00:02:02 to 00:04:37; PDF p.1 to p.2).
- Most technology infers an outcome (the athlete can run, has recovered) rather than measuring it; do not let the group agree its way past that (00:04:06 to 00:04:37).
- Meeting techniques: the rugby coach who sits silent then asks questions designed to unravel the plan; Weber turning staff against each other to see what survives; "five minutes, data only, no grand final pressure" (00:05:04 to 00:07:32).
- The AFL calf case: recurrent fatigue tears the coach understood intellectually but not emotionally; the fix was the doctor walking in and saying "stop everything", a different messenger for the same conclusion (00:08:04 to 00:10:00).
- Kahneman, adversarial stress testing and OODA orientation all say the first answer is not necessarily the one to act on, and a working system must be re-reviewed as staff, technology and knowledge change (00:10:01 to 00:13:42); see Framework 9.

## Frameworks and tools taught

### 1. The Five Integration Breakpoints (6A; Cheat Sheet p.1; Workbook p.4; 6A Summary p.1)

A diagnostic for any past decision where sound technical work did not change the outcome. Tick which broke: (1) Language gap: no shared framework for status, readiness or risk, including philosophical gaps where the words are understood but the models differ. (2) Decision pathway gap: no pre-agreed route for who collects, who reviews, where it goes next, what triggers a conversation. (3) Authority gradient: a senior figure overrides sound input without challenge or explanation. (4) Relationship deficit: the decision maker does not trust or understand the source; Weber treats this as the practitioner's responsibility to pre-educate. (5) Process absence: no meeting, gate or checkpoint requires the input to be addressed before the decision is finalised. Product: a named breakpoint for a specific case, plus what would have needed to be different.

### 2. The Diagnostic Questions (Workbook p.2; 6A 00:05:54)

Ask of yourself or each staff member: (1) When did your data last directly change a coaching decision? If none in three months, that is the answer. Trace the pathway. (2) How many people could accurately explain what the monitoring system measures and why? Estimate, name the gaps by role, state the cost. (3) What happens to your recommendations when you are not in the room: hold, modified, or disappear? (4, video only) How many could explain the return-to-run model and its decision gates?

### 3. The Real-World Failure Case reflection (Integration Workbook p.1 to p.5)

Sections A to E in order. A: define the integration problem as it appears in your environment; rate frequency (rarely / occasionally / regularly / almost always) and describe one observable signal. C: one case where technical quality was sound but the process produced a poor outcome: context and people; what the data indicated; what was decided instead and what overrode it; downstream cost to athlete, team, credibility, department. Optional table for multiple cases (Situation / What the data said / What happened instead / Downstream cost). D: locate the break against the five breakpoints; one-off or recurring and what has blocked resolution; what would have needed to be different (a process, relationship, language, structure or moment). E: complete "The one integration failure in my current environment that I most need to resolve is..." and bring it to the live session. The workbook states the rest of the module is built as responses to this case.

### 4. Encoding Realignment by scenario pre-commitment (6B; Part A PDF p.1)

Pick a common presentation (Weber uses a grade 2A hamstring). Before it happens, with every discipline in the room, write: how it will be assessed; the checkpoints; day-by-day expectations and tempo; the realistic return-to-performance timeline; who acts at each handover (for example day four to running staff); criteria for adapting off the plan. The output is a document the staff built together, which is what the coach sees ("this is the plan, these are the checkpoints"), and which is the reference for judging whether a deviation is a reasoned challenge or someone working outside the system. Repeat for performance progressions. Health check: can the physio describe what the strength coach will do next week, and vice versa.

### 5. First-meeting operating statement and SOPs (6B 00:11:43 to 00:12:22; Part A PDF p.2)

When inheriting a department, the first group meeting sets the encoding framework: who you are, what you do, how the department will operate, that you were hired to install a system rather than remove people, and that everyone will work to it. SOPs follow and are positioned as the way to find out who can work inside a collaborative system, and the transparent basis for escalating anyone who cannot.

### 6. The Translation Audit and the Option A / Option B choice (6C; Part B PDF p.1 to p.2)

List every concept you re-explain to a second and third audience in the same week; each is a gap. For each gap choose the route: line in the sand or education through workshops and internal CPD. Decide honestly who teaches it: Option A, you have the technical depth and stand up and explain the framework; Option B, you hire or empower the person who does and trust them, and do not defer to someone because it is easy. Agree in advance how contested metrics are framed in this environment. Product: an education plan sized to the resources you actually have.

### 7. The Six-Stage Decision Pathway and Five-Point Audit (6D, transcript only)

Stages: (1) data capture: GPS, force plate, RPE, clinical assessment, observation; (2) quality control: protocol followed, conditions consistent, anomalies caught; (3) analysis: thresholds, baselines; (4) interpretation: this number means the athlete is in this state; (5) communication: presenting to the person who acts; (6) decision and action.

Failure points and audit questions:

1. Dirty data (between 1 and 2). Unit not worn correctly, plate not zeroed, protocol skipped, and it sits in the database for weeks. Ask: who owns quality control and what does the check specifically consist of? If the answer is "nobody, it's informal", that is the finding.
2. Expertise gap (between 2 and 3). Data reliable but the analyst lacks the framework: normal-limit changes flagged as severe, a 50 ms RFD change on shoulder external rotation treated as an emergency. Ask: who set the thresholds, where were the defaults inherited from, is it written in a software platform, who reviews it, and is there a high-clarity handover when staff change?
3. Interpretation gap (between 3 and 4). A number is reported and the meeting moves on. Often caused by collecting more than the system can process. Ask: does it stop at the number, and who is there to handle it?
4. Communication gap (between 4 and 5). Technically precise, operationally opaque. Ask: what do you lead with, the method, the number or the recommendation? Apply the 20-second rule and a pre-built delivery structure for the coach.
5. Authority gap (between 5 and 6). Clear recommendation, no gate, never becomes a decision. Ask: is there a pre-agreed process that requires technical input to be formally addressed before return to play or selection is finalised? If not, recommendations are "advisory at best, optional at worst".

Product: name the single failure point costing the most decision quality each week (not the one that implicates someone) and fix it first. Keep written notes on every recommendation and decision.

### 8. The Grey Zone build, seven steps (6E; Grey Zone Workbook p.1 to p.12; Grey Zone Summary p.2 to p.7)

Run in order; the diagnostic leads into the design, which leads into the operating protocols.

Step 1, People Profile (Workbook p.2 to p.3). Map every staff member in the physio-S&C interface: Knowledge level (Handbrake: low knowledge, defaults to assumption, needs close supervision; Pawn: has knowledge but relies on instruction, hesitates at transitions; Practitioner: competent in own domain, collaboration depends on openness; Operator: high knowledge, autonomous, check for territorial bias) crossed with Behaviour (Misaligned: works against departmental logic; Coaster: present but passive under pressure; Catalyst: drives collaboration, anchor your protocols here; Beacon: sets the standard, amplifies or, if misaligned, undermines). Combinations needing extra structure: Misaligned x Operator; Beacon (Misaligned) x any Handbrake; two Practitioners with different domain biases; Pawn S&C + Operator Physio. Combinations that self-organise: Beacon x Catalyst; Operator x Operator with explicit handover points; Catalyst x Practitioner. Write the biggest risk in this specific pairing and the level of structure it needs.

Step 2, One Operational Logic (Workbook p.4; Summary p.3). Facilitate and record the agreed position (not individual opinions) on six domains: hamstring rehab markers; running readiness criteria (quality of movement versus quantity of exposure); return to full training threshold (what tests, who signs off); data we trust in-house; data we do not act on in isolation; what "athlete ready" means. Leave a row blank if unresolved; the blank is the priority.

Step 3, Rehab Phase Ownership Map (Workbook p.5; Summary p.4). For Return to Function (acute / post-surgical), Return to Run (loading), Return to Play (performance rebuild), Return to Competition: who owns it, who contributes, transition criteria, escalation required. Weber's reference: medical/physio owns RTF with S&C running parallel conditioning ("physio controls direction, S&C does not wait"); S&C owns RTR in most environments unless an exceptional running physio changes the calculus; RTP shared per pre-agreed criteria; RTC department-lead sign-off with immediate communication to the head coach. Pre-agree before any athlete is injured.

Step 4, Cross-Check Method (6E 00:07:43; Summary p.4). Even when S&C owns the phase, ask the physio to account for it. If the physio can relay the rationale, communication happened; if not, it did not. This is how you verify the model is running rather than assumed.

Step 5, Decision Empowerment Checklist (Workbook p.6; Summary p.5). For seven decision types (progress loading within agreed programme; regress loading; remove athlete from a field session; modify a published session; progress to next rehab phase; seek external specialist referral; return athlete to full contact) mark Yes/No for physio can act, S&C can act, must escalate to department lead. Skipping this produces overreach (Operator knowledge without role boundaries) or paralysis (Pawn behaviour in a Practitioner role, holding athletes back waiting for permission never withheld).

Step 6, Communication Protocol (Workbook p.7; Summary p.5 to p.6). For each decision event (athlete removed from field session; phase progressed; phase regressed or paused; specialist referral; return to full training cleared) fill in who is told, how fast, via what channel. Rules: the operationally responsible person owns the communication; the list is pre-defined per decision type; anything touching field presence is immediate, not end of session, not email; escalation triggers are pre-agreed so escalation is never a surprise. Then write the single biggest communication failure point and the one protocol change that fixes it.

Step 7, Walkthrough Exercise (Workbook p.8 to p.9; Summary p.6 to p.7). Choose one real or well-built hypothetical case. Physio and S&C coach each answer, in front of each other: what does progress look like; key risks right now; what data do you trust; time constraints; where do you need the other discipline most; what would cause you to pause or regress. Mark two or three divergence points. For the top one write the integration protocol: who owns this moment; what criteria determine the outcome; what is handed over and to whom; who can change the programme; who must be informed; what goes to the department lead without exception.

Finish with the Grey Zone Master Checklist (Workbook p.10 to p.11): 22 boxes across People Diagnosis, Operational Logic, Phase Ownership, Decision Empowerment, Communication, Ongoing Operations. "A blank box is a structural risk." Re-run after any staff change or mid-season.

### 9. Structured dissent toolkit (Podcast 6; Structured Thinking PDF p.1 to p.8)

- 10th Man Rule: when consensus forms, one person has the formal, protected obligation to argue the opposite. OBP application: designate that voice in the Kaigi decision log before RTR or programme calls are logged (PDF p.6).
- Six Thinking Hats (de Bono): White facts only; Red gut feel without justification; Black what could go wrong (the 10th Man hat); Yellow best case; Green alternative paths; Blue process control, who owns the decision and what is the review trigger. Everyone wears the same hat at the same time (PDF p.2 to p.3). Weber's lightweight version: "five minutes, data only".
- Pre-Mortem (Klein / Kahneman), three steps: state the decision; project forward ("it is four weeks from now, he is re-injured, what happened?") with each person writing independently before discussion; collect and group the failure scenarios and use the most credible to add contingencies before committing (PDF p.3).
- System 1 / System 2: Go/No-Go and Kaigi exist to force slow thinking onto decisions staff would otherwise make on pattern recognition, especially when a situation looks familiar but is not (PDF p.4).
- Red Teaming, five questions: under what conditions does this monitoring system give false confidence; what would have to be true about this athlete for our RTR assessment to be wrong; where are we relying on a single source; what are we not measuring and does the decision assume it is fine; if a different department looked at this data what would they conclude. Inter-departmental version: medical reviews performance decisions, S&C stress-tests medical thresholds (PDF p.4 to p.6).
- OODA loop: orientation (the department's "concept") is the underrated failure stage; accurate data through a stale filter still gives a wrong decision. Ask when you last reoriented your monitoring assumptions (PDF p.5 to p.6).
- OBP Bias Prompt Analysis, four layers to run before a decision is logged (PDF p.6 to p.7): (1) Recognition: what do we know, facts only; (2) Assumption audit: what are we treating as stable that might not be, when did we last check our concept; (3) Inversion: assign a 10th Man to argue the opposite and record the argument; (4) Pre-mortem close: "if this decision is wrong in four weeks, what happened?", record the top two answers in the decision log as review triggers.

## Deliverables / exercises

1. Integration Problem Workbook (5 pages): sections A to E per Framework 3, ending with the one-sentence closing statement for the live session.
2. Translation gap identification: 6C (00:02:31) refers to "the workbook associated with this lab". No such workbook is in the course folder; the Part B PDF is prose. Framework 6 is the reconstruction.
3. Decision Pathway audit (6D, 00:10:52 to 00:12:11): trace one recent important decision through all six stages, name the costliest failure point, assign an owner and a specific check. No PDF accompanies this lab.
4. Grey Zone Workbook (12 pages): People Profile and combination check (p.3); Operational Logic table (p.4); Rehab Phase Ownership Map (p.5); Decision Empowerment Checklist (p.6); Communication Protocol (p.7); Walkthrough table and divergence points (p.8 to p.9); Master Checklist (p.10 to p.11). Complete the People Profile first; design for the real environment; revisit after any staff change.
5. Structured Thinking: watch World War Z as a priming device (podcast 00:13:36; PDF p.6), then run the four-layer Bias Prompt Analysis on a live return-to-play or programme decision and record the review triggers. The PDF closes with: what is your department's current concept, when did you last audit it, how old is the filter you run monitoring data through (p.8).

## Key quotes

- "It's typically not a knowledge problem. It's an integration problem." (6A, 00:01:00)
- "It's not just about what I can do. It's about what I can get my team to do." (6A, 00:11:59)
- "If your recommendation changes as it moves up the chain, there is likely an integration leak." (Integration Cheat Sheet, p.1)
- "As a technician, I probably did a good job, but as a leader, I didn't." (6B, 00:14:27)
- "Translation is not just inconvenient. It is a performance leak inside the organisation." (Module 6B Part B PDF, p.1)
- "If you're more than 20 seconds away from getting an actual recommendation or coach, it's going to be lost." (6D, 00:07:56; transcript wording)
- "Otherwise, recommendations become advisory at best and optional at worst." (6D, 00:10:43)
- "The gray zone is not something we eliminate. It's something we organise." (6E, 00:12:16; also Grey Zone Workbook p.1)
- "Unowned zones always fill with assumption." (Grey Zone Workbook, p.12)
- "Don't wait for someone brave enough to raise the concern. Build the mechanism that makes raising it expected, protected, and logged." (Structured Thinking PDF, p.7)

## Source confidence

## Applicability notes

- The grey zone at Baylor is Athletic Medicine (athletic trainers, team physicians) to Athletic Performance, with Applied Performance on the data and analysis side of both. Weber's SEC example (new performance staff who share everything meeting incumbent medical staff who share nothing) is the closest case to a U.S. university structure, and his answer is a first-meeting operating statement plus written SOPs, not a turf negotiation. One adjustment: the team physician holds legal clearance authority in the college model, so the Rehab Phase Ownership Map should give Athletic Medicine the clearance gates at Return to Function and Return to Competition regardless of who owns operational progression in between.
- The Decision Empowerment Checklist and Communication Protocol are the fastest wins for athlete-availability decisions. Fill the seven-row empowerment table for one sport (who can pull an athlete from a field session, who can progress running exposure, what must reach the Director), then the five-row communication table with the head coach's notification path explicit and immediate. The course's line that a correct decision nobody communicated is a structural failure fits the football staff's sensitivity to seeing an athlete walk off the field.
- The six-stage Decision Pathway audit maps directly onto Applied Performance's pipeline (Catapult and force plate capture, quality control, thresholds, interpretation, coach-facing reporting). Run the dirty-data and expertise-gap questions (who owns QC, where were thresholds inherited from, is there a handover when staff change) on the current monitoring stack before the next staff transition, and adopt the 20-second recommendation-first rule as the standard for coach-facing reports.

- The One Operational Logic table is where the department decides in advance which data can trigger a unilateral decision and which need triangulation. For Baylor that means agreeing in writing where GPS exposure, force plate asymmetry, isometric strength and clinical assessment sit relative to each other in return to play, so a single metric or a dominant personality cannot impose its bias mid-pathway.

Before a return-to-play decision is logged, run the four layers and store the top two pre-mortem answers as review triggers. This gives Applied Performance a defined dissent role in the room that is procedural rather than personal.
